likely_phishing: Do not click links, open attachments or reply. If the user already did, treat it as an incident (see the steps marked 'if clicked').
Report the message to the security team and keep the original (.eml with full headers) as evidence; do not forward it as plain text.
Block the sender address and the domains/URLs below at the mail gateway and web proxy, then search other mailboxes for the same sender, subject, URL or attachment hash.
If the user clicked or opened anything: reset their password, revoke active sessions, check MFA methods and mailbox rules, and isolate the device if an attachment was opened.
suspicious: Hold the message and do not click or open anything until it is verified.
Verify with the claimed sender through a different channel (phone number from the directory, not from the email).
If it cannot be verified, treat it as likely phishing and follow those steps.
benign: No action needed. If the user is still unsure, ask them to confirm the sender through a separate channel.

indicators.title: Reply-To goes to a different domain than From
indicators.description: Replies would go somewhere other than the address the message claims to come from.
response: Do not reply; a reply would reach the Reply-To address, not the sender shown.

indicators.title: Return-Path (envelope sender) domain differs from From and nothing aligned vouches for it
indicators.description: Bulk senders legitimately use their own bounce domain, so this is only reported when no aligned DKIM or SPF pass exists.

indicators.title: Display name contains a different email address than the real sender
indicators.description: Mail clients show the display name prominently; putting another address in it is a classic trick.

indicators.title: Display name uses a brand name but the sender domain is not that brand's
indicators.description: The visible sender name claims a well-known brand, the actual domain does not belong to it.
response: Report the impersonated brand if it offers an abuse mailbox.

indicators.title: Display name matches a protected person or team, but the domain is not ours
indicators.description: An executive, finance, HR or IT help-desk name is used from an address outside the organisation's domains.
response: Confirm any request with the real person or team using a known phone number or chat.

indicators.title: Free-mail address using the name of a protected person, team or brand
indicators.description: Organisations rarely write from free webmail accounts, and attackers often do.

indicators.title: Sender domain imitates a protected brand or our own domain
indicators.description: The domain is a near-miss (typo, homoglyph or added word) of a brand or organisation domain.
response: Add the lookalike domain to the mail gateway block list.

indicators.title: No Message-ID header
indicators.description: Every normal mail server adds one; some scripts and spoofing tools do not.

indicators.title: Message-ID is malformed
indicators.description: Not in the form <unique@domain>.

indicators.title: Message-ID domain is unrelated to the sender
indicators.description: Only reported when nothing aligned vouches for the sender.

indicators.title: Date header missing or unparseable
indicators.description: Mail servers add a valid Date; many forged messages do not.

indicators.title: Date header is later than the time the mail was delivered
indicators.description: The sender's clock claims a time after delivery.

indicators.title: Date header is much older than the first delivery hop
indicators.description: A message dated weeks before it was first handled can be a replay or a forged header.

indicators.title: No Received headers
indicators.description: A message that crossed a mail server always has at least one Received header.

indicators.title: Received timestamps go backwards or show a very long delay
indicators.description: Hop timestamps should increase from origin to delivery; reversed or hours-long gaps suggest forged hops or replay.

indicators.title: Origin hop's HELO name does not match its reverse DNS
indicators.description: The sending host introduced itself with a name unrelated to its DNS name, or has no reverse DNS.

indicators.title: Unusually long Received chain
indicators.description: Many relays can indicate forwarding or relay abuse.

indicators.title: SPF failed: the sending server is not authorised for the envelope domain
indicators.description: The domain's SPF policy does not list the IP that delivered this message.

indicators.title: SPF softfail
indicators.description: The sending IP is probably not authorised (policy '~all').

indicators.title: DKIM signature failed verification
indicators.description: A signature is present but does not validate, so the message was altered or forged.

indicators.title: DMARC failed for the From domain
indicators.description: Neither SPF nor DKIM passed in alignment with the visible From domain.

indicators.title: DKIM passed but for a different domain than From
indicators.description: The signature vouches for another domain, not the one the reader sees.

indicators.title: No SPF, DKIM or DMARC results available
indicators.description: Nothing in the message tells us whether the sender was authenticated.

indicators.title: Link points to a raw IP address
indicators.description: Legitimate services link to named hosts, not numbers (including decimal, hex or octal disguised IPs).

indicators.title: Link uses look-alike (homograph) characters
indicators.description: A punycode (xn--) host mixes scripts or imitates a brand using characters from another alphabet.

indicators.title: Link domain imitates a brand or our own domain
indicators.description: Typosquatting by edit distance, digit/letter swaps (0/o, 1/l, rn/m) or the brand name on a different domain.

indicators.title: Brand name used inside a domain it does not own
indicators.description: For example brand-secure.example or login-brand.example.

indicators.title: Brand domain appears as a subdomain of someone else's domain
indicators.description: For example brand.com.evil.example: the real domain is the last part, not the first.

indicators.title: Link goes through a URL shortener
indicators.description: The real destination is hidden until clicked.

indicators.title: Link text shows one address but the link goes to another
indicators.description: The visible text names a domain that is not the domain the link points to.

indicators.title: Link uses a top-level domain often abused for phishing
indicators.description: Heuristic only: many abused TLDs are cheap or free.

indicators.title: Link contains user@ credentials syntax that hides the real host
indicators.description: In https://trusted.com@evil.example/ the real host is evil.example.

indicators.title: Link carries a redirect parameter to a different site
indicators.description: An open-redirect style parameter (url=, redirect=, next=) points to another domain.

indicators.title: Login/verify wording in a link to an unrelated domain
indicators.description: Words like login, verify or secure in the path or host of a link that is not on a known domain.

indicators.title: Link uses a javascript: or data: scheme
indicators.description: These run or embed code instead of opening a normal web page.

indicators.title: Very long or deeply nested link
indicators.description: Extremely long URLs or many subdomain levels are used to hide the real domain.

indicators.title: Attachment is an executable or script type
indicators.description: By extension or by content (Windows executable, script, shortcut, disk image).
response: Do not open the attachment. If it was opened, isolate the device and run a full scan.

indicators.title: Attachment content does not match its file extension
indicators.description: The first bytes identify another format than the extension claims.

indicators.title: Attachment has a double extension (document name, executable type)
indicators.description: invoice.pdf.exe shows as invoice.pdf when extensions are hidden.

indicators.title: File name contains a right-to-left override character
indicators.description: U+202E makes part of the name display reversed, hiding the real extension.

indicators.title: Office document that can contain macros
indicators.description: Macro-enabled type (.docm, .xlsm, ...) or a document with a VBA project inside.
response: Do not enable macros or content. If it was opened, report it so the device can be checked.

indicators.title: Archive lists an executable or script inside
indicators.description: Read from the archive's directory only; nothing was extracted.

indicators.title: Password-protected archive
indicators.description: Encryption stops mail scanners from looking inside, which attackers rely on.

indicators.title: Message body gives a password for the attached archive
indicators.description: Handing the recipient the password is how encrypted malware archives are delivered.

indicators.title: HTML or SVG file attached
indicators.description: Attached web pages run in the browser from a local file, bypassing link scanning.

indicators.title: HTML attachment builds a file in the browser (HTML smuggling)
indicators.description: JavaScript Blob / base64 decoding plus an automatic download assembles the payload on the victim's machine.
response: Do not open the HTML file. If it was opened, check the Downloads folder and isolate the device.

indicators.title: HTML attachment contains a password form
indicators.description: A login page delivered as a file is a credential harvester.

indicators.title: SVG attachment contains script
indicators.description: SVG images can carry JavaScript that redirects or drops files.

indicators.title: PDF contains JavaScript or launch actions
indicators.description: Active content inside a PDF is unusual for invoices and letters.

indicators.title: Attachment hash is on the known-bad list
indicators.description: The SHA-256 matches a hash you listed as malicious.
response: Quarantine every copy of this message.

indicators.title: Urgent or threatening wording
indicators.description: At least two pressure phrases (deadline, suspension, final notice).

indicators.title: Asks the reader to verify, confirm or reset credentials
indicators.description: Credential-harvesting wording. Legitimate password-reset mail uses it too, so it only scores lightly.

indicators.title: Invoice, payment or bank-detail wording
indicators.description: Finance wording used in invoice scams and payment diversion.

indicators.title: Gift-card request
indicators.description: Asking staff to buy gift cards and send the codes is a well-known scam.
response: Tell the user not to buy anything; confirm with the real person by phone.

indicators.title: Business-email-compromise style request
indicators.description: At least two of: availability check, favour, secrecy, new bank details, wire/payment request, 'in a meeting'.
response: Verify any payment or bank-detail change by phone with a known number before acting.

indicators.title: Asks the reader to scan a QR code
indicators.description: QR codes move the link onto a phone, out of reach of link scanning. This tool cannot decode QR images.
response: Do not scan the QR code. Ask the user whether they did; if so, treat the destination as a phishing site.

indicators.title: Generic greeting ("Dear customer")
indicators.description: Mass mailings do not know your name.

indicators.title: Credential or urgency lure combined with a deceptive link
indicators.description: A pressure or credential lure plus a lookalike, mismatched, IP-based or userinfo link.

indicators.title: Executive impersonation combined with payment or gift-card wording
indicators.description: The classic CEO-fraud pattern.

indicators.title: Claims a protected identity and fails authentication
indicators.description: The sender impersonates a brand or protected name and SPF or DMARC failed.

indicators.title: Sender domain authenticated and aligned (DMARC pass, or aligned DKIM or SPF pass)
indicators.description: Reduces the score: the message really came from the domain it shows. Attackers can authenticate their own domains, so this is a small credit.

indicators.title: Has a List-Unsubscribe header
indicators.description: A hallmark of bulk mail from real senders (it can be forged, so the credit is small).

indicators.title: Asks the reader to 'enable content' or macros
indicators.description: Macro malware relies on persuading the user to switch protection off.
response: Do not open the document or enable content; delete the message after reporting it.
